:::{#def-sequence-limit}
#### Limit of a sequence

A real number $L$ is the **limit** of a [sequence](sets-functions.qmd#def-sequence) $(a_n)$ of real numbers,
written $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L$ or $a_n \to L$,
if for every $\tolout > 0$ there is a natural number $N$ such that

$$\abs{a_n - L} < \tolout \quad \text{for every } n \ge N.$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-sequence-limit}
#### The limit of a sequence

$a_n = \frac{1}{n}$ has limit $0$.
Given $\tolout > 0$, take $N$ to be any natural number larger than $\frac{1}{\tolout}$.
For every $n \ge N$, $\abs{\frac{1}{n} - 0} = \frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{N} < \tolout$.
For example, with $\tolout = 0.01$, take $N = 101$:
every $n \ge 101$ has $\frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{101} < 0.01$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-convergent-sequence}
#### Convergent sequence (converges)

A sequence $(a_n)$ of real numbers **converges** to a real number $L$ if $L$ is its limit (@def-sequence-limit).
A sequence that converges to some real number is **convergent**.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-convergent-sequence}
#### A convergent sequence

$a_n = \frac{1}{n}$ converges to $0$, because $0$ is its limit (@exm-sequence-limit),
so $a_n = \frac{1}{n}$ is convergent.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-divergent-sequence}
#### Divergent sequence (diverges)

A sequence that does not converge (@def-convergent-sequence) to any real number **diverges**.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-divergent-sequence}
#### A divergent sequence

$c_n = n$ diverges.
For any real number $L$ and $\tolout = 1$,
every $n > L + 1$ has $\abs{n - L} > 1$,
so no $N$ works.
For example, with $L = 5$, every $n \ge 7$ has $\abs{n - 5} \ge 2$.
It diverges to $\infty$:
for every real number $M$, every $n \ge N$ has $c_n = n > M$
when $N$ is a natural number larger than $M$.

:::
